title: The sleeping palace
hook: he wakes at night to see the musicians asleep and sprawled; the glamour is gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula: a son is born, and his name means a fetter. Your line was love, and the fear inside it. Did you loosen your grip by one finger? Day thirty-six, and a new week: the going forth.
screen: `RAHULA — LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: The end of a party, two in the morning. The lights come up. The music stops. The room that looked magical an hour ago is suddenly just a room: sticky cups, a torn streamer, someone asleep on the couch with their mouth open. Nothing has changed except the light, and yet everything has. In the story, the prince comes home on the night his son is born. The palace throws him a celebration: dancers, singers, musicians, all for him. But his mind is somewhere else, and he falls asleep in the middle of it. The performers, seeing no one watching, lie down where they are and sleep too. Sometime in the night, the prince wakes up. Today, the sleeping palace.
screen: `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `A PARTY FOR THE PRINCE.` → `HE WAKES IN THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The lamps are still burning, and by their light he sees his palace as it really is. The later telling doesn't spare the details. Dancers sprawled across the floor, instruments dropped beside them. Some snoring. Some grinding their teeth. Some talking in their sleep, mouths open, clothes in disarray. The same people who were beautiful and dazzling a few hours ago are just tired bodies now. The telling says the great hall looked to him like a burial ground. And earlier that same evening, one more thing happened. A young woman watching him ride by had sung a little verse: happy is the mother, happy the father, happy the wife of a man like this. The word she used for happy can also mean cooled, at peace, and it's related to nibbana. The prince heard it and thought: what is it that's truly cooled? And he knew. The fires of wanting, gone out. Put those two moments together and you have today's teaching. The glamour was never in the palace. It was a spell, a way of seeing, and in one night it broke. Buddhists have a word for this feeling, samvega: a jolt of clear-eyed urgency, the shock of seeing ordinary life plainly. It isn't disgust with people. The dancers did nothing wrong. It's the moment the prince stops being enchanted, and starts being awake to what he'd been looking at all along.
screen: `THE HALL BY LAMPLIGHT.` · `JUST TIRED BODIES NOW.` · `HAPPY, COOLED, AT PEACE.` · `SAMVEGA — A CLEAR-EYED JOLT.` · then, large: `THE SPELL BREAKS.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in right now, as if the lights just came up. Pick one ordinary thing: a chair, a lamp, a pile of laundry, a phone. Look at it as if you've never seen it before. Its shape. Its color. What it's for. What it cost, what it will become when it wears out. You're not trying to dislike anything. You're just seeing it without the story you usually tell about it. Then close your eyes and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The sleeping palace. The night the prince woke to see his glittering hall by plain lamplight, and the spell of it was gone.
Your line: the spell breaks. Today, see one familiar room with fresh eyes, your kitchen, your desk, your car, and notice what's actually there. Day thirty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell the sleeping palace as the night of the great departure, and teachers point to samvega, the jolt of seeing life plainly, as a healthy spur to practice rather than a reason for gloom.

fork.setup: you wake in the night and the dazzling hall looks like a room of tired, sprawled bodies. what's happening?
options: the spell has broken: you're seeing it plainly.
fork.reveal: nothing had changed but his seeing. the later telling says the hall looked to him like a burial ground, and that night he decided to leave.

original.note: Pali: a stirring, a sense of urgency, the shock of seeing life clearly.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince got tired of parties.
what it means: in one night the glamour fell away and he saw his life plainly. the spell broke.
what a scholar hears: in the Nidanakatha, Kisa Gotami's verse turns on nibbuta, cooled, at peace; the sleeping hall is likened to a charnel ground; samvega names the stirring.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): Kisa Gotami's verse and the sleeping palace

notes: The young woman (Kisa Gotami, a cousin, not the Kisa Gotami of the mustard seed) is left unnamed to avoid confusion with day 74. Confirm.
Her verse is paraphrased (nibbuta nuna sa mata...). In the Nidanakatha she sings as he rides home, before the sleeping-palace scene. Confirm the order.
The prince sends her a pearl necklace in the telling; omitted.
Samvega introduced here as a Buddhist term; confirm the gloss 'a jolt of clear-eyed urgency'.
